statehood-criteria.what:
A state, in international law, is what most people mean by a country. Countries needed a shared way to say what counts as one, because treaties, embassies and borders only work between entities that treat each other as real. The usual checklist comes from Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty that defines what a state is. It asks for four things, a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries. Article 3 adds that a state exists whether or not others recognize it.

In ordinary terms, a founder would need people who actually live in one place as their home, an area with known limits, an authority that really runs that area, and foreign governments willing to talk. The tests are harder than they look. A platform with rotating staff struggles on population. A site with no territory fails the second test. The capacity to deal with others depends on other countries being willing to do so, which brings back the need for acceptance that Article 3 seems to set aside.

The record shows how this plays out. In 1978 a court in Cologne, asked by a German who called himself Sealand's prime minister to let him drop his German citizenship, held that Sealand was no state. Somaliland has governed most of the land it claims since 1991 and had no recognition from any UN member until Israel's in December 2025.

Declaring independence is a separate matter. In 2010 the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, advised in the Kosovo case that general international law contains no applicable ban on declaring independence. That leaves open whether a declaration achieves anything.

territory-law.what:
A country needs land or something like it, and the old way to get land was to occupy a place that belonged to no one. Over the last century countries have closed almost every such place by treaty, largely so that they would not fight over it. Almost every place outside a country is now closed to claims.

At sea, the rules are in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. Artificial islands get no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has (Article 60(8)). The high seas cannot be claimed (Article 89), and the deep seabed cannot be taken as anyone's own (Article 137). So a person who builds a platform in open ocean has a structure with no surrounding water of its own and no claim to the ocean under it. The Antarctic Treaty, which governs that continent, takes no new claims (Article IV). The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, bars any country from taking over space (Article II).

The old route has its own limit. Occupying land that belongs to no one is a method used by countries, so a private person cannot use it directly. In its Western Sahara opinion, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, said the practice of countries at the relevant time did not treat land inhabited by socially and politically organized peoples as qualifying.

That leaves two strips of land, Bir Tawil and Gornja Siga, each between neighbors with border guards. Vit Jedlicka declared Liberland on Gornja Siga in 2015. Croatia has detained visitors since then, and in 2023 a camp built there was taken down and removed with police watching. In 1971 backers of the Republic of Minerva piled sand on a South Pacific reef, and on 15 June 1972 Tonga proclaimed the reefs its own with its neighbours' backing.

un-admission.what:
The United Nations is the main club of countries, and joining it is the clearest public sign that the world accepts a place as a state. Article 4 of the UN Charter, the UN's founding treaty, opens membership to peace-loving states, by a decision of the General Assembly on a recommendation from the Security Council. The rule exists because the founders wanted the most powerful countries to have a say over who joined.

The steps run in order. A place applies, and the Security Council votes first. The Council needs nine of its 15 votes, with no veto from any of the five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the UK and the US). If that succeeds, the Assembly needs a two-thirds majority of those present and voting. That means 129 yes votes out of 193, if all vote. A founder would therefore need to win over dozens of foreign governments and avoid opposition from any one of five.

Being widely accepted does not guarantee a seat. On 18 April 2024 a proposal for full UN membership for Palestine won 12 votes in the Council, with 2 abstentions, and failed on a US veto. Kosovo is recognised by 110 UN members and belongs to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and it is not a UN member. Taiwan has its own government and about 23.3 million people, and it lost China's seat in 1971 when members voted that Beijing's government was China's rightful representative.

South Sudan was the last to join, in 2011, after an independence process. Palestine and the Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church, sit as non-member observers. Self-declared projects have tried the application as a gesture. The founders of Nutopia asked for UN recognition in 1973, and the art project Elgaland-Vargaland applied for membership in 1994. Neither became a member.

micro-precedents.what:
People often assume a real country must be large, and a small project can seem absurd by comparison. The record says otherwise. Size is no bar. Small countries counted by the World Bank in 2024 include Tuvalu with 9,646 people, Nauru with 11,947 and Palau with 17,695. San Marino, Monaco and Liechtenstein have 34,000 to 40,000 people. The treaty that defines a state, the Montevideo Convention of 1933, asks for a permanent population and gives no minimum number.

It helps to see why those places are accepted. All three of the smallest hold natural land and are recognized by others. Their people have lived there for generations. Each has a government that actually runs the place, and other countries deal with it. Their size matters less than those facts.

A new project's obstacle therefore lies in territory and consent, since a population of about 10,000 is already enough for a UN seat in practice. A founder would be mistaken to think that gathering 10,000 people solves the problem. Asgardia, a self-declared space nation, reported more than 290,000 citizens in 2019, many times the population of Tuvalu, and no state or UN body recognises it, because those people live in other countries and have no land in common. Slowjamastan, a patch of California desert, had more than 25,000 citizen applications by March 2026, and nobody lived there as of February 2025.

The opposite also holds. A very small group that holds real territory still needs others' consent. Sealand has held its sea fort since 1967, and it has a single caretaker living there. A list of tiny recognized countries is useful for showing that a small state is possible, and it says nothing about how to become one.

legal-personality.what:
A treaty is a written agreement between countries, and it works much like a contract between companies. A contract only binds if both sides are legal persons able to sign. International law has a similar idea. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the treaty on how treaties work, applies to agreements between countries, and its Article 6 says every country can make them. The ability to make such agreements is what lawyers mean by legal personality.

Anyone can print a document with the word treaty at the top. To other countries, a 'treaty' signed by an unrecognized place would appear to be a private document. This matters because nearly every other requirement here runs on treaties, including extradition, air services, post, tax and membership of the International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for radio coordination. A founder without this ability cannot get into those systems as a country, and each one must be reached through a company or a friendly state.

Some bodies other than countries have gained this standing through long history. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with no land, signs treaties and reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, while Wikipedia gives 115 states. It began in the 11th century and kept its status after losing Malta in 1798, which a new group cannot copy.

Declaring independence does not supply this ability either. The 2010 opinion on Kosovo by the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, concerns only whether a declaration broke the law. The ability to make treaties comes from other countries treating a place as a state. Wirtland, an internet-only project, proposed in 2010 to ask Nauru for a piece of its territory, and no land is known to have changed hands.

iso-3166.what:
Computers and clerks around the world need short, agreed labels for countries. ISO 3166 is the international list of two- and three-letter country codes, used by banks, shipping, airlines, web domains and passports. France is FR, for example. When a bank's software asks which country a customer lives in, it usually picks from this list. A place that is missing from it can run into trouble at the most ordinary moments, since many forms and systems have no box for it.

The list has 249 codes assigned. A body called ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, publishes the standard, and an office called the Maintenance Agency keeps the list. The agency relies on someone else's judgment of who is a country. As reported on Wikipedia from the Maintenance Agency, the only way in is to be registered in either the UN Terminology Bulletin Country Names or the UN Statistics Division's Standard Country or Area Codes. Entry therefore depends on the UN. This account rests on that secondary source, and ISO's own page was not reviewed.

A founder cannot apply and persuade the agency directly. The practical sequence starts at the UN lists, and a self-declared place has no way to reach those lists on its own.

Kosovo shows how an accepted place copes without a code. It uses XK, a code from the 'user-assigned' range, which sits outside the official list. Those codes exist for private use, and organizations can agree among themselves to treat one as meaning a place. That works only because the organizations choose to go along, and Kosovo's recognition by 110 UN members gives them a reason. A micronation can type any letters it likes into its own website, and outside systems have no reason to accept them.

cctld.what:
Web addresses end in a suffix, called a top-level domain. Some are general, such as .com, and some belong to a place, such as .fr for France. The place-based ones are called country code domains. A new country would naturally want one, as a mark of status and as a home for its government sites.

Country web domains are tied to the ISO 3166 list of country codes. RFC 1591, the 1994 document that set the policy, says the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), which manages these domains, 'is not in the business of deciding what is and what is not a country', and that the ISO list was picked because ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, has a procedure for that decision. The engineers who built the internet wanted to stay out of arguments over borders, so they handed the question to someone else.

A new '.xx' domain therefore follows only after a place gets its ISO code, and that code in turn depends on UN lists. A founder cannot file a request with IANA and argue the case.

There is a simple workaround that has real limits. Anyone can still buy an ordinary .com or a domain under another country's code, which means your web address sits under another registry's rules. That registry can apply its own terms and the law of its home country, and it can take the name away. Self-declared projects all live this way. Wirtland stamped its web address on its silver coins, and Bitnation ran from an ordinary web domain that had been sold by August 2022, when the project was considered defunct. The address belongs to whoever holds the registration, and a declaration of sovereignty makes no difference to the registry.

ip-addresses.what:
Every device on the internet is reached through a number called an IP address, in the way a house is reached through a street address. Someone has to hand out those numbers so that no two devices share one. That job falls to five regional registries, AFRINIC for Africa, APNIC for Asia-Pacific, ARIN for North America, LACNIC for Latin America and the Caribbean, and RIPE NCC for Europe, the Middle East and parts of Central Asia. A country does not need a seat at the UN to use the internet, but its networks need a block of these numbers from somewhere.

ARIN, the North American registry, says businesses, nonprofits or government entities are eligible, including individuals who meet the legal requirements of the country where they do business. The normal route is therefore a registered legal entity in a real country. The registries deal with applicants as organizations under an existing country's law, and they have no process for deciding whether a self-declared place is a government.

A self-declared state has two choices. It could apply through a company it registers elsewhere, or it could rely on an upstream provider, a company that supplies its internet connection and lends it addresses. Either way, the provider's home country can cut service, because the company is under that country's law and courts.

HavenCo shows the problem. It was an internet hosting company on Sealand, the sea fort off England, founded in 2000 to keep customers' data beyond the reach of other countries' courts. Its own company was bought in Britain and later moved to Cyprus, and a law professor who wrote its history found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's internet links more than any government did. CyberBunker, which called itself a republic while hosting websites from former military bunkers in the Netherlands and Germany, was raided by 600 police in 2019, and German courts convicted its operators.

iso-4217.what:
Banks do not write out "United States dollar" when they record a payment. They use a three-letter code, USD, from an international list called ISO 4217. EUR is the euro. These codes matter because banks and trading systems use them to book payments, and the software that does this expects each amount to carry a code it recognizes.

SIX, the Swiss exchange group, is the official Maintenance Agency for the list, meaning the office that keeps it, and calls itself the only recognized, authoritative source on currency codes. The purpose is practical. If every bank used its own label, payments between banks would keep failing or going to the wrong currency.

Suppose a new place prints its own notes. Without a code, its currency would have no standard listing on normal payment systems. A bank in Frankfurt would have no standard way to book a payment in it. That appears to limit the currency to local paper money or a private token. Sealand has issued coins since 1972, nominally pegged 1:1 to the US dollar, and the micronation Atlantium sold coins and banknotes in its imperial solidus. Both are self-issued money of that local or collectable kind.

A founder would have to find out who may apply and on what terms. ISO's own description of who may apply, ISO being the International Organization for Standardization that publishes the standard, was not reviewed for this entry, so that point remains open here. In practice the code is a small part of the problem, because a code alone gives no bank a reason to deal in the currency. Banks would still want a licensed central authority behind it and a way to swap it for other money.

own-currency.what:
Money works because people expect others to accept it. A founder has three choices, to issue a new money, to use someone else's, or to use crypto. Each brings its own trouble.

Printing notes costs little, and Minerva, Sealand and New Utopia all produced a currency or pictures of one. Legal tender status means courts in your place accept the money to settle debts, which helps only where you have courts others respect. Outside the project, the question is simpler. Outsiders will take your money only if they can swap it for something. A shopkeeper in the nearest port will want dollars or euros, so a settlement that buys its food and fuel abroad needs outside money anyway.

Using a foreign currency avoids printing but brings dependence on foreign banks. Somaliland, which has run its own government since 1991, issues its own Somaliland shilling. The Murrawarri Republic, declared in Australia in 2013, uses Australian money. Atlantium's imperial solidus and the raam, issued by the Global Country of World Peace and accepted by some businesses in Iowa and the Netherlands, stayed small and depended on people's goodwill.

Crypto looks like a way around this, yet the businesses that convert crypto to dollars are regulated in their home countries. Your people therefore end up subject to those countries' rules at the point of exchange. A token can be passed freely among members, but the rent, the doctor and the ship's fuel usually have to be paid in ordinary money. Tokens also raise the risk of securities law if they are sold with a promise of profit. In 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) sued over New Utopia's bond offer, which also promised currency returns as high as 200 percent.

fatf-travel-rule.what:
When money moves between banks, governments want to be able to follow it, so that criminals and terrorists cannot hide behind anonymous transfers. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), an international body, writes the standard that most countries' anti-money-laundering rules follow. FATF is not a court and does not arrest anyone. Its members write the standard, and countries then turn it into national law, which their banks must obey.

Its Recommendation 16, known as the Travel Rule, requires financial institutions and virtual asset service providers (crypto businesses) to share who sent and who receives a transfer. The information travels with the payment, like a label on a parcel. For cross-border transfers above USD/EUR 1,000, the 2025 revision requires the name, account number and country and town of the person receiving the money. The revisions take effect at the end of 2030 and reach crypto firms indirectly, through FATF's Recommendation 15 on new technologies. This account comes from a law firm's summary and from Elliptic, a crypto analysis firm, and not from FATF's own text.

For a founder, this has an effect that is easy to miss. A resident of a self-declared place who receives a transfer must give a name, an account and a country and town. A place the bank's system does not list may not be accepted, so the person's real legal address comes into the record. A bank or crypto business that cannot get the information has a reason to refuse the transfer.

Holding crypto does not remove this, because the rule covers the businesses that convert it. A project that promises members financial privacy from every government is promising something its banking partners cannot lawfully provide, and its members meet the rule each time money enters or leaves through a regulated firm.

mica.what:
Crypto tokens were sold for years under rules that differed from one European country to another. The European Union replaced that with one set of rules for all its countries. The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) sets uniform rules for crypto-assets not already covered by financial law, including asset-referenced and e-money tokens, which are types of stablecoin (crypto tokens tied to the value of something else, such as a currency).

Two requirements matter most. It requires white papers, the disclosure documents for a token, which tell buyers what they are getting and what the risks are. It also requires official approval for service providers, the businesses that offer exchange or custody of tokens. A firm that wants to keep customers in the EU must therefore apply for a licence and follow its conditions. Firms already operating before 30 December 2024 could continue only until 1 July 2026 or until a decision on their licence.

Any citizen token sold to people in the EU now falls under these rules. Even when a project is based outside the EU, its customers and exchanges may be inside it. Suppose an online nation based nowhere in particular sells a membership token, and a buyer in Germany uses a licensed exchange. The exchange would be expected to ask for the disclosure document and to drop a token that does not comply.

A founder who wanted to sell in Europe would have to prepare a compliant white paper and work with licensed firms, or stay out of the EU market. Calling the token a citizenship does not change what it is if it is offered like an investment. Praxis, whose reported $500 million facility from the crypto firm GEM Digital depended on listing tokens on a public exchange, shows how much some projects rely on the markets that such rules govern.

genius.what:
A stablecoin is a crypto token tied to the value of a currency, usually the US dollar. The promise is that one token can always be swapped for one dollar. That promise is only as good as the money held behind it, and a run on a poorly backed token can wipe out its holders. The US GENIUS Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-27) was passed to set rules on this.

It says US issuers of these tokens need approval from a state or federal regulator and must hold at least one dollar of permitted reserves for each dollar issued. Issuers above $50 billion must file audited statements. In ordinary terms, an issuer must be able to show that the money is there.

Foreign tokens are also covered. Exchanges in the US may offer foreign stablecoins only under set conditions, and the Treasury may arrange 'reciprocal' deals with places that have comparable rules. An unrecognized place appears to have no regulator for the Treasury to deal with. So a micronation that issues a dollar-backed token would seem to have no way onto US exchanges under its own flag, whatever reserves it holds.

A founder who wanted such a token would likely have to issue it through a regulated firm in a real country and follow that country's rules, which gives up the independence the token was supposed to show.

The details are still being written. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), a US bank regulator, has issued final rules, and the Treasury proposed more in 2026. A project relying on any reading of the Act should expect changes.

correspondent-banking.what:
A bank in a small town cannot have an account at every bank in the world. So banks use a chain. International payments travel between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A payment from a village in one country to a shop in another may pass through two or three of them, usually including a large bank in New York or London for dollars and pounds.

Each bank in the chain is legally answerable for what passes through it, so it wants to know who is at the other end. It relies on the other country's banking law and supervisor to have checked the customer. A new place with no banking law or supervisor gives them no one to rely on.

The Financial Stability Board, an international body that monitors the financial system, reports a steady fall in those relationships. Active correspondents dropped 3.9% in 2016, 4.1% in 2017 and 3.4% in 2018, with US dollar links falling fastest and smaller, higher-risk places hit hardest. This retreat is called de-risking. Newer data has not been reviewed. Even recognized small countries have been cut off, so a place with no recognition starts behind them.

Without a correspondent, your people cannot receive a wire transfer. A founder would need a bank in a real country willing to serve the project as an ordinary customer, under that country's rules. Members would keep their accounts in their home countries. Melchizedek claimed to have sold about 300 bank licences by the end of the 1990s, and in 1991 shell banks tried to get loans with fake securities and were shut down, which helps explain why banks treat licences from self-declared places with such suspicion.

swift.what:
SWIFT is the messaging network banks use to instruct payments. It describes itself as a member-owned cooperative under Belgian law, serving more than 12,500 institutions in over 200 countries and territories. When one bank tells another to pay out money, the instruction usually travels over this network in a standard format, much as a telegram once did. It carries the messages between banks, and the money itself moves through the accounts banks hold with each other.

Because so many international payments depend on these messages, governments have treated access as a form of power. Regional law binds SWIFT, and it says that as a Belgian company it must follow EU regulation. In March 2012 an EU regulation made it disconnect sanctioned Iranian banks. In March 2022, an EU regulation banned the service for seven Russian banks. A network that large would not be able to ignore such an order, and a bank removed from it has to find slower and costlier ways to pay.

SWIFT's own eligibility criteria are not quoted here. The practical path for a new place is a licensed bank, which needs a licensing authority other countries accept. Suppose a founder sets up a "national bank" on a platform and asks to join. The first question would be which authority licensed and supervises it. A self-appointed ministry's stamp gives no answer that another bank's compliance office can accept. Melchizedek's bank licences, about 300 claimed sold by the end of the 1990s, show why that question gets asked.

Crypto payment systems avoid SWIFT, and they then run into the exchange and stablecoin rules described in the other entries. At the point where members want to turn tokens into the local money for rent or food, a regulated business and a bank are usually involved again. In practice a project's members would use their existing accounts in real countries, which reach SWIFT through those banks, and they would remain under those banks' rules.

fatf-grey.what:
Banks need a quick way to judge how risky a country is. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that sets anti-money-laundering standards, provides one by listing places with weak rules. It reviews countries' laws and enforcement, and those with serious gaps go on a list officially called jurisdictions under increased monitoring and widely known as the grey list. A country on the list agrees to a plan to fix the gaps, and it comes off when the gaps are closed.

The list has real costs. A paper at the International Monetary Fund by Kida and Paetzold estimates that being on this 'grey list' cuts capital inflows by about 7.6% of GDP, the yearly value of a country's economy. Banks and investors treat the listing as a warning, and they demand more checks or leave.

After the June 2026 meeting, 22 places were on the list, and an industry summary reports four removals in October 2026 (Bulgaria, Monaco, Côte d'Ivoire and DR Congo), which would leave 18 if none were added. Iran, North Korea and Myanmar are on a separate high-risk list.

A self-declared place faces a different and perhaps harder position. A place FATF has never assessed would appear to have no clean record to show banks. It cannot point to a review it passed, and to a bank's compliance office an unknown place may look worse than a listed one. Building the machinery that would satisfy a reviewer takes laws, a financial intelligence office, supervisors and prosecutors, which a small project does not have. A founder would have to depend on a bank in a real country and that country's standing, with the project's members treated as higher-risk customers.

passports-icao.what:
A passport is a request from one government to others to let its holder pass, and it works only because governments have agreed to honour each other's. Border machines add a further layer. The strip of letters at the bottom of a passport page is written to a common standard, so that a reader in any airport can check it. Doc 9303, a standard from the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency for civil flying, sets that format.

Part 3 of the standard says the codes for issuing countries come from the agency that keeps the ISO 3166 country code list, plus separate lists for bodies such as the UN and INTERPOL. Recognized passports therefore link back to the UN lists that feed ISO 3166. ICAO has 193 member countries. Joining under the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, means being a UN member, or winning four-fifths of ICAO's Assembly with UN approval (Articles 92 and 93).

Printing a booklet in this format still gets no code on these lists, so machine readers and border systems would appear to have no entry for it. A founder can make something that looks right, and the officer at the desk then has to decide.

Acceptance has to be arranged government by government. The Nansen passport of 1922, about 450,000 issued, worked because governments agreed in advance to honour it. The Haudenosaunee passport, in use since at least 1923, is judged case by case. Japan admitted a delegation on it in 2005, and Britain refused it for a lacrosse team in 2010. Garry Davis's World Passport, with no such agreement, led to repeated arrests and expulsions for its founder. In 2002 a group travelling on Elgaland-Vargaland passports was detained in Estonia and sent back to Sweden the next day.

camouflage-passports.what:
Some travel documents are not forgeries of real passports and are not valid either. A camouflage passport looks real but names a country or body that does not exist. A fantasy passport is a similar novelty, not valid for travel. The difference from a real passport is simple, because no government stands behind either one and no other government has agreed to honour it.

These documents draw two kinds of buyers. Some want a souvenir of a project they like. Others hope to pass a border or open a bank account, and that is where criminal risk begins. Sealand's passports were called fantasy passports by the Council of the EU, according to Wikipedia. The EU glossary itself has not been reviewed. In 1997, the Bates family, who run Sealand, revoked them after finding an international money-laundering ring using them. The Dominion of Melchizedek sold passports for up to $3,500, and three people posing as its officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998. A listing does not always mean fraud. The Haudenosaunee passport, issued by a people with a long claim of their own, is also listed by the European Union as a fantasy passport.

The legal risk does not depend on copying a real country's passport. In US law it is a crime to falsely make 'any passport or instrument purporting to be a passport' intended for use, and to use one (18 USC 1543). Using one at a border may bring charges under such laws, and the person also faces being refused entry and sent back.

A founder who wants to issue documents safely would label them plainly as commemorative or membership cards, would never suggest they work for travel, and would warn members not to present them to any officer. Members still need their real passports for every actual trip.

citizenship-tax-us.what:
Most countries tax people according to where they live. The United States is unusual in taxing its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live. The Supreme Court upheld this in Cook v. Tait (1924), for a citizen living in Mexico with Mexican income. The court accepted that the benefit of citizenship goes with the person, and so does the tax. Americans abroad must still file.

The duty follows citizenship, so joining a micronation (a self-declared small country) appears to change nothing. Suppose an American moves to a platform in open ocean and takes a new "citizenship" from its founders. In US law that person is still a US citizen, because only the United States decides who holds its nationality. A return is still due each year on income from anywhere in the world, including wages paid in tokens.

Anyone hoping to live on a platform tax-free therefore faces a tax return every year until they formally give up US nationality. Leaving is possible, and it has its own costs, covered under renunciation. There is a further danger. Giving it up without holding another nationality leaves a person stateless, because a self-declared country's papers do not count as a nationality for other governments. The State Department warns that a stateless person lacks the protection of any government and may have difficulty traveling. Mehran Karimi Nasseri, who lived in a French airport terminal from 1988 to 2006 with no accepted papers, is an extreme example of what lacking usable documents can mean.

Other countries' citizens should check their own rules, since many tax by residence, and a move may change their position. Moving does not end the duty to file for an American who keeps the passport.

renunciation.what:
Americans who want to escape US tax on their worldwide income have one lawful exit, which is to give up citizenship formally. The government charges a fee for this and, for some people, applies a tax on leaving. The tax exists so that wealthy people cannot build up gains while citizens and then leave without paying on them.

Giving up US citizenship formally costs a government fee. The fee was $2,350 from 2015 until a final rule published in March 2026 cut it to $450, so the $2,350 figure often quoted is out of date.

Separately, 'covered expatriates' pay an exit tax. That means anyone with $2 million or more in net worth, or average income tax above $211,000 a year (2026 figure), or who has not certified five years of tax compliance. The last test catches people of modest means who are behind on their paperwork. Covered expatriates are treated as selling all their assets the day before leaving, after an exclusion of $910,000 for 2026. So someone holding a house or shares that have risen in value owes tax on the gain as if they had sold them, though nothing was actually sold.

A founder would also need to think about what comes after. A person who renounces with no other nationality becomes stateless, which brings difficulty traveling and no government to protect them, since a micronation's papers count for nothing with other governments. The practical order is to hold a real second citizenship first. Garry Davis gave up his American citizenship at the US embassy in Paris in 1948, saying he was a citizen of the world, and he was regularly arrested and expelled in the 65 years he then travelled.

fatca-crs.what:
A person might hope that moving money offshore hides it from the tax office at home. For many people that stopped being true some years ago. Countries now get account information directly from foreign banks, under two main systems, one American and one international.

Foreign banks report US account holders to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the US tax agency, under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA). Americans must also report foreign financial assets above set limits. The general limit on Form 8938 is $50,000, which may be higher in some cases, and failing to report carries a $10,000 penalty. So the same account may be reported twice, once by the bank and once by the customer, and the two reports can be matched.

Many other countries swap account data under the Common Reporting Standard of the OECD, a club of mostly wealthy countries. Banks collect each customer's tax home, and governments send the data to one another. A report on the Global Forum, the international group that oversees this exchange, gives 171 million accounts worth nearly EUR 13 trillion, 172 member countries and territories, and about EUR 135 billion in extra revenue. These figures come from a news summary, and the OECD's report page did not show them.

Your bank therefore tells your home tax office you have the account, whichever flag you live under. A founder cannot change this by issuing a new passport, because a bank that opens an account asks for a real tax residence and proof of it. Claiming to be tax resident in a micronation gives the bank nothing it can accept, and a refusal or more questions are likely. A project running its own "bank" outside these systems would have no correspondent bank to reach the outside world. The practical result is that members remain visible to their home countries for as long as they keep money in ordinary banks.

ship-flag.what:
Open ocean has no police of its own, so the law of the sea gives each ship a home country. On the high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, a ship needs a country's flag, with a 'genuine link' to that country (Article 91 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans). The flag country's law then applies on board. That lets everyone know who is responsible for a ship, and it gives other ships a country to complain to.

A ship with no flag is exposed. Warships may board on suspicion of no nationality (Article 110(1)(d)). A ship using several flags may be treated as having none (Article 92(2)). In US drug law, a 'vessel without nationality' includes one whose claimed registry is denied by the nation named, or whose captain makes no claim when asked (46 USC 70502). Article 110(1) gives five grounds for boarding in all. A flag issued by a micronation would appear to give no protection, since no recognized nation stands behind it.

A real flag has its own price. It means living under that country's law and its duties on safety and crew (Article 94). Choosing the flag of a country with no coast is allowed (Article 90), since any country may run a register.

Women on Waves shows the rule in use. Its ship flies the Dutch flag and holds a Dutch permit, and it relies on Dutch law once beyond a country's territorial sea. MS Satoshi shows the other side. In 2020 no insurer would cover a stationary residential ship, which would mean no crew, the loss of its safety rating and the loss of its flag, and the owners sold it.

boarding-offences.what:
A ship on the open ocean is usually left alone by every warship except those of its own flag country. That is the general rule under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. A few acts have long been treated as a danger to everyone, and they lift the protection.

Three acts open a ship to foreign warships regardless of flag, in the broadcasting case only if the warship's country has legal power under Article 109. The first is piracy. Any country may seize a pirate ship and try those aboard (Article 105), and piracy covers violence or detention for private ends against another ship or in a place outside any country's control (Article 101). The second is the slave trade. Suspicion allows a warship to stop and inspect (Article 110), and a slave who reaches any ship is free (Article 99). The third is unauthorized broadcasting. Any country receiving the signal or suffering interference may arrest the person and seize the equipment (Article 109). Five kinds of country can prosecute unauthorized broadcasts.

Funding a project through a pirate radio station therefore invites arrest. Pirate radio has a real history here. Radio Caroline broadcast to Britain from ships from 1964, and Britain's 1967 Act made it illegal for British subjects to supply or advertise on such a station. Dutch authorities raided its last ship in 1989. Roy Bates, founder of Sealand, had just been convicted for running such a station on a fort.

Piracy can be wider than people expect. In the Sea Shepherd case, a US appeals court ruled in 2013 that 'private ends' is far broader than money, so an environmental group that rammed whaling ships and threw acid could be accused of it. A founder who plans to detain anyone at sea or block another ship should know this.

crime.what:
Every society needs to answer who deals with a theft, an assault or a death. A self-declared place might write a criminal code and appoint a judge, and it may feel natural to think that settles the matter. Other countries would not see it that way. With no recognized court, the answer is any country with a link to the case.

Several countries can have such a link at once. The country whose flag or register covers the structure applies its law. A person's own country often does too. US law reaches 'any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation' for offenses by or against a US national (18 USC 7(7)). Other countries may act on piracy or broadcasting.

Suppose a resident on a platform is hurt in a fight and the attacker is locked in a storeroom by the founders. Your own court's verdict would not be accepted by others as binding, and locking someone up on your platform appears able to count as kidnapping or unlawful detention under the law of their home country. The founders could thus become defendants themselves. Sealand's owners have acted as a court in just this way. In 1978 they retook their fort from a German lawyer, Gernot Pütz, and fined him 75,000 Deutsche Marks, a penalty no recognized court stood behind.

Courts have sometimes declined to reach these places. In 1968 a judge at Chelmsford ruled that British firearms law did not apply to Sealand, because Parliament had never extended it beyond the three-mile limit. Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles in 1987, which now covers the tower, so that gap has closed.

The practical result is that a founder cannot offer residents a working justice system of its own. Serious crime must be handed to a real country's police, and that fact should be planned for in advance.

extradition.what:
Extradition is the handing over of a person to another country to face charges. It exists because a country's police generally cannot go and make arrests on another country's soil, so governments make agreements to send suspects to each other. It runs on treaties between governments. In US law, a judge's power starts with 'a treaty or convention for extradition' with a foreign government (18 USC 3184).

A place with no treaties cannot ask for anyone back. If a resident steals from a project and flies home, the project has no process it can start. A letter to a foreign ministry from a self-declared state would have no standing.

The rules also work against the project in the other direction. Countries where your citizens travel can still hand them over to third countries under their own treaties. A fugitive from one country therefore gains little from a flag, and your residents can be arrested as soon as they land in a port. Sooner or later most people on a platform need to go ashore for medical care or supplies.

The history shows this risk. Simon Mann, arrested in Zimbabwe over the 2004 plot against Equatorial Guinea, served three years there and was then extradited to Equatorial Guinea. Paul Watson, formerly of Sea Shepherd, was arrested in Greenland in July 2024 on a Japanese warrant and freed in December after Denmark rejected extradition, which shows that the decision rests with the country holding the person. In Thailand's 2019 case, the navy raided a floating home and filed a police complaint over an offense it said carries life imprisonment or death. The couple had left the cabin before the raid. How the case ended is not known.

A founder should therefore tell residents plainly that their legal exposure travels with them.

force-record.what:
Any place claiming to be a country has to ask what happens when a real navy or police force arrives. A founder might hope that international law protects small places. Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, the UN's founding treaty, bars force in its members' international relations against 'any state', which appears to offer an unrecognized project little protection. The ban protects states, and neighbours do not treat a platform or a camp as one. To them, sending officers is ordinary law enforcement on what they regard as their own territory or area of interest.

The record is short and consistent. Italy took Rose Island 56 days after its declaration and bombed it. Tonga claimed the Minerva Reefs within weeks and removed later occupiers with troops. Thailand raided a seastead, a floating home at sea, in 2019 and raised the death penalty. Croatia has jailed and fined visitors to Liberland.

Sealand survived an armed takeover by hired mercenaries in 1978, and Britain later placed it within its waters by law. At the time the fort lay outside Britain's three-mile limit, and an English court had ruled in 1968 that it had no power over the tower.

In Antarctica and on the Moon, military bases are barred by treaty for the countries that have joined, so a private armed force would meet that ban through its home country.

Defending a project by force also creates new criminal exposure. Michael Bates's shots near a boat in 1968 led to a court case, and armed standoffs like the one at Ganienkeh in New York in 1990 draw police attention. A founder has little realistic way to match a navy. The usual end comes with officers, a tow boat or a demolition order, and the founder then faces a court in the neighbouring country.

rescue.what:
Far from land, a medical emergency becomes a question of who will come and where they will take you. The law of the sea has an old rule on this, grown from the risks all sailors share. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, ship captains must rescue people in danger at sea (Article 98), so a nearby ship should come, and coastal countries run search-and-rescue services for their waters. No flag or citizenship is required to be saved.

The rescue does not bring independence with it. After rescue you land in someone else's country, under its law. A person wanted there, or lacking valid papers, then has that problem to face in addition to the injury.

Space has a similar rule with a narrower reach. If spacecraft crew land in distress on a member country's territory or on the high seas, members must help them and return them to the launching authority (Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, Articles 2 to 4, and Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, Article V). That authority is a country or a qualifying international organization, so a self-declared state appears to have no standing. On the Moon or Mars, no outside rescue is realistically close.

Ordinary medicine is the more frequent issue. A hospital of your own is a cost in the budget, and specialist care means going ashore. A small settlement must pay for a doctor and medicine, and for a boat or aircraft to reach a hospital, and insurers may refuse the risk. MS Satoshi's owners found in 2020 that no insurer would cover a stationary residential ship. A founder would have to plan on someone else's hospitals, under someone else's rules, and residents should keep valid passports for that trip.

sanctions.what:
Governments sometimes try to change another country's behaviour, or to punish individuals, by forbidding their own people to deal with them. These rules are called sanctions. They are enforced mostly through banks and against the people who do the dealing, which is why they follow a person across borders.

The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the US sanctions office, binds all US citizens and permanent residents wherever they are located, plus US entities and their foreign branches. The property of blocked people must be frozen. OFAC publishes tables of civil penalties each year. EU sanctions cut seven Russian banks from SWIFT, the bank messaging network, in 2022, and the rule extended to entities they own by 50% or more. The ownership rule means a company can be caught even when its own name is not on a list.

A place outside every country may attract exactly the wrong customers. A person under sanctions could see a self-declared place as a route around the rules, for instance through a passport, a token or a company. Any US person who helps a listed person at your project therefore appears to take on personal legal exposure, wherever the project sits. An American running the project's accounts, selling that person a cabin or giving legal advice might be affected, even on a platform in open ocean.

A founder would need to check members and buyers against the sanctions lists, as ordinary businesses do, and refuse those who appear on them. Selling citizenship online with no checks carries a clear risk, and the outside banks a project depends on will expect such checks. Melchizedek's passport sales and Sealand's revoked passports, used by a money-laundering ring according to the Bates family, show that paper of this kind attracts people seeking to hide.

securities-fraud.what:
A security is an investment sold to the public, such as a share or a bond, where the buyer hands over money and hopes to profit from what others do. Governments regulate these sales closely, because buyers cannot easily check what they are being told. Sellers usually have to register the offer, or qualify for an exemption, and they must tell the truth.

Selling a stake in a future country to the public can count as selling securities. In 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of investment markets, sued Lazarus Long, born Howard Turney, over a $350 million bond offering at 9.5% interest for 'New Utopia', a Caribbean nation that had not been built. The court froze the funds, and in January 2000 he consented to a permanent injunction, a court order banning the conduct. He had raised $24,000, and the order to hand the money back was waived because he could not pay. The charges were under Securities Act Sections 5 and 17(a) and Exchange Act Section 10(b). The website that made the offer was enough to reach buyers and bring the regulator.

Citizenship tokens with a promised return carry the same risk. Calling the buyer a citizen does not settle the question, because regulators look at what is really being offered. A founder who sells land, bonds or tokens with talk of rising value should expect this law to apply wherever buyers live.

The Dominion of Melchizedek is the larger warning. One of its investment schemes took over $4 million from at least 1,400 people, and its founder, Mark Pedley, pleaded guilty to share manipulation in 2010. The safer course is to sell only what is delivered, such as a membership or a souvenir, with no promise of profit, and to take legal advice in each country where buyers live.

lunar-deeds.what:
The Moon has been for sale on the internet for decades, and many people own a certificate for an acre of it. It is worth knowing what they have bought. Dennis Hope's Lunar Embassy has sold acres of the Moon since 1980. He read the Outer Space Treaty, saw that it barred nations from taking land in space, and concluded that this left individuals free. He filed a claim, sent it to the United Nations and treats the lack of reply as approval.

Sales have been large in number and small in price. Discover magazine reported 4.25 million buyers and over $9 million in sales at $19.99, and National Geographic reported 2.5 million plots at $22.49.

The law gives these deeds nothing to rest on. A deed records a transfer of land from someone who owns it, under a government that keeps property records. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, bars any country from taking over the Moon, and the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with few members, bars private property in the surface for its members. A seller therefore has no country whose law could back the title. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, issued a statement warning that such deeds could mislead individuals. No court or government registry backing them has been found. Ram Jakhu, a space law professor at McGill University, says the treaty was written to block such claims.

Buyers receive a printed deed. It works as a novelty gift and gives no right to enter, use or exclude anyone from any part of the Moon. A founder who plans to sell lunar land as an investment rather than a novelty would also meet the securities and fraud rules that apply to any other sale of investments.

launch-licence.what:
A rocket can kill people on the ground and damage other spacecraft, so a government must approve a launch before it happens. In the United States that job belongs to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US aviation regulator. A US launch needs a licence from the FAA, as does any launch by a US citizen outside the US (51 USC 50904). The licence rules are in 14 CFR Part 450. An American founder cannot avoid the rule by launching from another country.

The applicant has to show the launch can be done safely and has to pay for harm if something goes wrong. The licence holder must carry insurance for harm to others, sized to the 'maximum probable loss' and capped at $500 million or the most available on the world market at a reasonable cost (51 USC 50914 and 14 CFR 440.9). The payload must also comply with US law, and the government can block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds.

A US launch therefore brings US supervision with it. In 2016 the company Moon Express got the FAA's first favourable review of a commercial payload meant to land on the Moon, after the agency consulted the State Department and NASA, and that mission never flew. Swarm Technologies shows the other side of the rule. In 2018 it launched four tiny satellites on an Indian rocket after being refused a US radio licence by the Federal Communications Commission, another regulator, which still had reach over an American company. It paid a $900,000 penalty.

Asgardia, a self-declared space nation, reached orbit in 2017 only because US companies launched its 2.8-kilogram satellite on a NASA-funded mission, and the satellite stayed under US authority.

space-registration.what:
Every object sent into orbit needs a country on record as responsible for it, in the way a car needs an owner and a plate. The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, requires a launching country to register each object and give the UN its orbit and purpose (Articles II and IV). This helps identify what is up there and who answers for it.

The list has a legal effect that is decisive for founders. The registering country then keeps legal power and control over the object and anyone aboard (Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, Article VIII). So a space station registered by the United States is under US power, and a person living aboard remains under that power.

This is the central obstacle for any orbital nation. Only launching countries, and international organizations that accept the Convention, run these registers (Articles II and VII), and being on a country's register puts you under that country. The Convention has 77 members. It appears to give private people no way to register themselves. A founder might try to choose a country with lenient rules, an idea lawyers have compared to flags of convenience in shipping. That would still put the craft under a real country's authority, and the practice has not been tested in any court.

Asgardia called itself the first nation with all its territory in space in 2017. Legal scholars disagreed, because US companies launched its satellite and it stayed under US authority, and the satellite burned up in 2022 with no one aboard. An interstellar ship would be in the same position, because Article VIII gives no distance at which the country's control ends.

liability-convention.what:
If a rocket stage falls on a town, someone must pay. Because governments launch or allow launches, and because a private company might not have the money, the countries agreed that they themselves would answer for it. Under the Liability Convention, the treaty on who pays for damage from space objects, a launching country must pay for damage its object causes on Earth or to aircraft, with no need to prove fault (Article II). In space, it pays only if at fault (Article III).

More than one country can be on the hook. Countries that launch together share the liability (Article V). A launching country includes one that launches, pays for the launch, or whose territory is used (Article I). So a satellite owned by a company in one country and launched from another may expose both governments. The Convention has 100 members.

A country exposed in this way appears to have good reason to require licensing and insurance before a launch. This is the plain explanation for why governments will not simply let a private group launch and declare its craft outside all law. The country whose soil was used stays liable whatever flag the owners claim. The US rule requiring insurance of up to $500 million or the most available at a reasonable cost is one such requirement.

For a founder, the effect is that every launch needs a government willing to carry this risk, and that government will set conditions in return. A self-declared space nation is not a party to the Convention, and it appears to have no standing to accept the duty or make a claim under it. Lawyers have warned that cheap registries might lead to more debris and danger, and a registry alone cannot remove the liability of the launching country.

spectrum.what:
Radio signals spread across borders, and two transmitters on the same frequency in the same area will garble each other. A spacecraft that cannot talk to the ground is useless, and many ships depend on radio too. So countries have long coordinated their use. Spacecraft and many ships need radio frequencies, which are coordinated by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio coordination.

Its founding treaty, the ITU Constitution, treats frequencies and orbits as limited natural resources (Article 44) and bars harmful interference (Article 45). National authorities submit notices of frequency assignments, which are entered in the Master International Frequency Register, the official global list. The ITU has 194 member countries. Countries outside the UN can apply only with the agreement of two-thirds of members under Article 2(c).

A self-declared state therefore needs a member to file for it, which puts that member's regulator in charge. Tonga shows how much a small member can do. From 1990 its company Tongasat filed for orbital slots, first 16, and the ITU agreed in 1991 after the request was cut to six. Tonga eventually held nine, and the plan was to rent each for $2 million a year. Its filing power came from being a recognized member. The venture later ended up in court, where a judge ruled in 2018 that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money, and how its appeal ended is not known.

The national regulator has real power. In 2017 the US Federal Communications Commission refused an experimental licence to Swarm Technologies, which launched anyway from India. Swarm paid a $900,000 penalty and agreed to file pre-launch reports for three years. Offshore radio also shows the risk. From 15 April 1970 Britain jammed the signal of the pirate station Radio North Sea International.

air-routes.what:
Countries control the airspace above their land, and in 1944 they agreed on rules that kept that control over who flies through it. Under the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, scheduled international air service needs special permission from each country flown over or landed in (Article 6). Non-scheduled flights have more freedom, but only for aircraft of countries that have joined the treaty (Article 5). This is why airlines rely on agreements between governments for their routes.

Aircraft are treated somewhat like ships. Every aircraft has one country of registration and must carry its marks (Articles 17 to 20). The Tokyo Convention, a 1963 treaty, says that country's law covers crimes on board, even over the open ocean. An aircraft flying over land no state owns therefore still carries a national legal system with it, and a registered flying platform would too.

An airline from an unrecognized place therefore cannot use these rights, since it has no member country behind it. A plane marked with a self-declared country's letters would have no registration that others accept. The workaround is to rely on aircraft registered in another country. That means a charter from a real operator under a real regulator, and that operator will not land where the authorities forbid it. Pilotless craft need separate permission (Article 8).

For a founder, reaching a project by air means depending on the country that controls the nearest airspace and on the country whose marks the plane carries. A plane on the ground is also within reach of local police. In 2004, police at Harare airport impounded the Boeing 727 carrying the Wonga Coup plotters, and Rajneeshpuram's airstrip in Oregon stayed under ordinary US law.

environment.what:
Building anything large in an untouched place can harm it, and damage crosses borders. So nearly every place outside normal national control has its own environmental rules, and a founder has to find out which apply. Each place has its own process. The rules mostly bind countries, and a country then applies them to its people.

Article 28 of the BBNJ Agreement, the treaty on marine life in waters outside any country's control, has required its members to assess the impact of planned activities in those areas since January 2026. An impact assessment is a study of what a project will do to the surroundings, made before work starts. Antarctica requires an assessment beforehand under Article 8 of the Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the Antarctic Treaty, and Article 7 bans mining. At sea, the London Protocol, a treaty on dumping, treats dumping as forbidden unless permitted. Members of the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, must avoid harmful contamination (Article IX), and COSPAR, an international space science committee, sets standards on protecting other planets.

These rules can bite on building. The South China Sea tribunal, a panel of judges under the law-of-the-sea treaty, held that building land at seven reefs breached a country's duties on the marine environment. A private group piling sand on a reef, as at Minerva in 1971, would appear likely to raise the same kind of concern today.

If your home country has joined these treaties, it may apply these rules to you through its own law. So a founder could be answerable at home for what is done far away. A self-declared place cannot exempt itself by not signing. A floating project near a coast must also deal with that coastal state's rules.

food-water-power.what:
A settlement outside every country still needs to eat. Declarations do not touch this problem, and supply is usually what ties a project back to the nearest port. No project in the published sources has produced its own food at scale.

The numbers for space show how much is at stake. A person needs about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day, according to NASA, and food use on the International Space Station (ISS) ran at 2.77 kg per crew member per day. The ISS has reached 98% water recovery, and it still relies on deliveries for tanks, water bags and food. The station has government budgets behind it and still depends on deliveries, so a private group should not assume it can do without them.

At sea, a platform needs a port. Fuel, spare parts, food and people arrive by boat, and the boat must leave from somewhere. Oceanix's Busan design, a planned floating district in South Korea, intends to make its own energy on site, though that remains a plan.

Dependence on a neighbor's port appears to give that neighbor leverage. Italy blockaded Rose Island after seizing it, to stop anyone from returning. Britain's 1967 law against pirate radio made it illegal for British subjects to supply such stations, and the Dutch banned supplying them from land in 1974. Radio Caroline's broadcasts at sea stopped in 1990 for lack of fuel and supplies. A neighbour does not have to send a warship. It can act against the suppliers on its own shore.

A founder would need to count the daily tonnage, contract with suppliers in a real country and accept that country's rules on what can be shipped. Farming and desalination can reduce dependence over time. Those systems still need parts that come from elsewhere.

population.what:
A country needs people, and the question of how many is more complicated than it looks. The Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty that defines what a state is, asks for a permanent population without giving a number. Permanent means people who live there as their home, as opposed to visitors or rotating workers. Tuvalu has 9,646 people, and that is enough for a recognized country.

Science has tried to estimate a working minimum for a place cut off from the world. A model by the researcher Salotti in the journal Scientific Reports puts the minimum for a self-sustaining Mars colony at 110, based on labor time and under strong assumptions. It is a calculation about keeping everything running, and it does not describe an actual settlement.

The rule of thumb from these cases is that a society can be small on paper, while a working one needs doctors, engineers, teachers and courts. A few dozen people cannot supply all those skills, and families will want schools and a hospital before they bring children.

Sealand shows the limit. Wikipedia reports one permanent resident as of August 2024, and the Minnesota Journal of Law, Science and Technology reported two in 2019. Online numbers can be misleading. Asgardia had over 500,000 sign-ups within three weeks and no one has ever lived in its territory. Mars One said 202,586 people applied in 2013, while a finalist said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. Free State Project pledges reached 20,000 in 2016, and about 6,232 people had actually moved by May 2022.

A founder should count people who have moved, along with what they do all day, and give less weight to names on a list.

cost-floating.what:
A floating city has to be built like a large ship or an offshore structure, then kept in repair against salt and storms for as long as people live on it. Nothing of this kind has yet been built at city scale, so published figures are all estimates for things not yet built.

The numbers vary widely. Oceanix Busan, in South Korea, was stated at $200 million in 2021, or $627 million at the developers' $10,000 per square metre, for 15.5 acres and 12,000 people. Freedom Ship runs as high as about $16 billion for 80,000 people and has stalled for decades. Pangeos is about $8 billion for 60,000. A law journal puts even a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million. By simple arithmetic on those numbers, the cost per resident runs from about $17,000 to $200,000 for the larger plans, and far more for a small platform.

Such estimates tend to move. Freedom Ship's own company gave US$6 billion in 1999 and US$11 billion by 2002, and later estimates reached $15 billion and $20 billion, with no ship built. Blueseed, which planned to lease a ship off California, assumed $18 million more would come in, and the project went on hold in 2013 when it did not.

Construction is only the start. A project also needs insurance, crew, port fees and repairs each year. MS Satoshi was bought in 2020 as a ready-made ship, and it was sold for scrap within weeks when no insurer would cover it as a stationary residence. The XLII cabin off Phuket, a far smaller home, was raided and towed away by the Thai navy in 2019.

A founder would need to plan on outside investors, who will ask what law protects their money. Without a real country's courts, that is a hard question to answer.

cost-orbit.what:
Getting anything into space costs money for every kilogram, because rockets burn huge amounts of fuel to lift it. That price sets the budget for everything else, so space planners count in dollars per kilogram.

The price has fallen a great deal. Jones, writing for NASA, calculated $54,500 per kg for the Space Shuttle to low orbit, and $2,720 per kg for SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket at its 2018 price of $62 million. By early 2026, a full Falcon 9 for one customer was about $74 million, or $3,246 per kg at full capacity. A shared flight starts at $350,000 for 50 kg. Voyager's filings imply $90 million for a Starship flight, once certified, according to Motley Fool's reading of them. The words once certified matter, since that figure is a projection.

Those are rocket costs alone. Food, at 2.77 kg a day, comes to about 1,000 kg a person each year, or about $3.3 million at the Falcon 9 rate, by simple arithmetic. That is one person's food for one year, before water, air, spare parts, medicine, the habitat itself or the crew's own flight.

A founder has to compare these figures with what backers can pay. Mars One estimated $6 billion for its first mission, built no hardware, and its company was declared bankrupt in 2019 with debts of about 1 million euros. MirCorp paid for one flight to the Mir station in 2000 and ran out of money when the dot-com crash hit its main backer. Asgardia's actual reach in orbit was a single 2.8-kilogram satellite. Every launch also comes with the licensing and insurance duties of the launching country, and a cheaper ride leaves those rules in place.

cost-station.what:
Living in orbit means keeping a sealed building in working order, with air, water, power and repairs, far from any shop. The running cost of that building is much larger than most people expect. The International Space Station (ISS) costs about $3 billion a year to run, according to NASA's Inspector General. It has many governments paying for it. A private settlement would have to pay in some other way, or build far smaller.

Private companies are now testing the market. Vast, a private space station company, has committed more than $1 billion to its single-module Haven-1 station, which has slipped to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027, and it had sold no crew seat as of that report. So a billion dollars has gone in before the first paying visitor.

The price of a visit gives another measure. Axiom, a private space company, gave a price of $55 million a seat for a 10-day trip to the ISS, plus NASA charges reported then as $2,000 per person per day for food and more for support. Those prices assume short stays, and a person who wanted to live in orbit would pay for flights, supplies and a share of the structure year after year.

Earlier ventures show what can happen. MirCorp signed up the paying passenger Dennis Tito and said it had $100 million in future business, but its money ran out and Mir was brought down from orbit in March 2001. Tito flew to the ISS instead.

A founder would also need a launching country's licence and registration, so the money would buy a home under that country's power. At these prices, private stays in orbit have been short trips for very wealthy people.

buyers.what:
Before spending on a new country, it is worth knowing who has actually paid for one in the past. A sign-up is free, and a dollar figure in a press release may be a plan. The published record is mostly online sign-ups and small purchases.

Lunar deed buyers number in the millions at about $20 each. Buyers receive a printed deed. Liberland reported hundreds of thousands of applications. Asgardia reported more than 290,000 citizens in 2019 and over 500,000 sign-ups within three weeks. Such sign-ups have not produced a settled population in either place.

Investors are a much smaller group, and they want a return. New Utopia raised $24,000 against a $350 million offer. Praxis's reported $525 million was mostly a $500 million facility from GEM Digital, conditional on listing tokens on a public exchange. Próspera, a special zone in Honduras, drew foreign investors, and its claim against Honduras has fallen from $10.775 billion to $1.63 billion. That zone had a real country's law behind it until the Honduran Supreme Court declared the zone laws unconstitutional in September 2024.

Some people pay for an actual stay or a real legal benefit. The Network School charged about $1,500 to $3,000 a month and had 266 foreign residents at its July 2026 inspection. Estonia's e-Residency, run by a real state, brought it nearly €125 million in direct revenue in 2025. Real second citizenship has a market too, as with the programme of St Kitts and Nevis, running since 1984.

The pattern for a founder is that people pay real money for things that work at a border or a bank, and pay small sums for symbols. A plan that needs thousands of paying residents has very little in this record to rely on.
